lesson.title: The Sensorimotor Stage: Learning Through Looking, Touching, and Doing
lesson.summary: In Piaget's first stage, from birth to about age two, infants come to know the world almost entirely through their senses and motor actions, gradually building toward the ability to represent things mentally instead of only acting on them directly.
lesson.body:
In Piaget's framework, the sensorimotor stage covers roughly the first two years of life, and its name describes exactly what is happening: infants' intelligence is expressed through their senses (seeing, hearing, touching, tasting) and their motor actions (grabbing, mouthing, shaking, dropping), rather than through internal, symbolic thought.

This stage builds directly on the reflexes described in the infant physical development chapter. Piaget proposed that infants begin with those built-in reflexive responses, like rooting and grasping, and gradually turn them into deliberate, repeated actions. An infant who accidentally shakes a rattle and hears a sound will often repeat the shaking on purpose, exploring what their own actions can make happen. Over the course of the sensorimotor stage, this kind of exploration becomes increasingly intentional and increasingly aimed at understanding cause and effect, such as deliberately dropping objects from a high chair to watch what happens.

The signature cognitive achievement of this stage is object permanence: the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they can no longer be seen, heard, or touched. Piaget observed that this understanding does not appear all at once but develops gradually across the sensorimotor stage, and it gets a full chapter of its own later in this unit because of how much research it has generated.

Toward the end of the sensorimotor stage, infants begin to show the first signs of mental representation, the ability to hold an image of something in mind even when it is not present. This capacity is what allows development to move into Piaget's next stage, the preoperational stage, where symbolic thought becomes the dominant way children make sense of their world. Along the way, many infants also show stranger anxiety and separation anxiety, often emerging somewhere in the second half of the first year, which many researchers connect to this same growing ability to mentally represent a caregiver who is not currently in view.
